<cell id="cell-0"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type># andesim: a hands-on tutorial

`andesim` is one command that drives the Andes RISC-V simulators. This
notebook teaches it by running **real commands** against the binary built in
this repo. Each code cell is a plain shell command - the `!` prefix (or a `%%bash`
block) tells Jupyter to run it in the shell - so everything here is exactly what
you would type in a terminal.

## The mental model: one run = MODEL x ENGINE ( x TRIGGER )

To run something you pick up to three things:

| Axis | Question it answers | Choices |
|------|---------------------|---------|
| **model**   | which simulators run, and how they combine | `fast`, `cycle`, `hybrid` |
| **engine**  | which concrete simulator binary            | `qemu` (built in) or `vsim:<cpu>` (discovered) |
| **trigger** | (hybrid only) where the measured region starts and ends | `marker`, `pc` |

The three models in one picture:

```
fast    QEMU only        fast (MHz speed), functional only, NO cycle count
cycle   one vsim only    cycle-accurate, but runs the WHOLE program in RTL (slow)
hybrid  QEMU  ->  vsim    QEMU fast-forwards; vsim measures only the region you pick
```

`hybrid` is the reason the tool exists: QEMU runs the boring parts quickly,
and the cycle-accurate vsim measures only the small region of interest (ROI).

> Note: this tutorial drives `andesim` (the C++ product). The retired
> Python `./hsim.py` survives only as the parity golden.</cell id="cell-0">
<cell id="cell-1"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## Setup

Prerequisites: the driver, the simulators, and the test fixtures are already
built (`build/andesim`, `verilator/build/sim_*`, `build/qemu/...`, the QEMU
plugin, and `tests/fixtures/*.elf`). If any are missing:

```sh
bash scripts/build_driver.sh      # the driver only
# or, everything:
source ./setup.sh                 # qemu + vsim + plugin + simpoint
make -C tests/fixtures -j         # the .elf fixtures
```

The single cell below is the only Python in this notebook: it finds the repo
root, switches to it, and puts `build/` on `PATH`, so every later cell can call
`!andesim` directly. (It walks up to the `build/andesim` binary, so there
is no hardcoded path - it works wherever the repo lives.)</cell id="cell-1">

Start with `--help`. The release surface is deliberately small: just `run`,

<cell id="cell-4">!andesim --help</cell id="cell-4">

<cell id="cell-9"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>`list engines` shows the concrete simulators. `qemu` is built in. The
`vsim:<cpu>` rows are discovered at runtime by scanning `verilator/build/` for
binaries that describe themselves, so building a new CPU config makes it appear
here with no code change.

- **KIND** is what the selector keys on: `functional` (QEMU) vs
  `cycle-accurate` (vsim). `cycle` and `hybrid` need a `cycle-accurate` engine.
- **VLEN** is the vector register width in bits (`-` means not reported).</cell id="cell-9">

ENGINE                 TYPE  KIND            XLEN  VLEN  DLEN  ELEN
qemu                   qemu  functional      64    -     -     -   
vsim:ax45mpv_mp2       vsim  cycle-accurate  64    512   512   32  
vsim:ax45mpv_premium   vsim  cycle-accurate  64    512   512   32  
vsim:ax46mpv_advanced  vsim  cycle-accurate  64    512   512   32  

<cell id="cell-11"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>> This repo has **five** cycle-accurate engines built. When more than one
> exists, `cycle` and `hybrid` cannot guess which to use, so you must name one
> with `--engine` (shown below). If only one were built, it would be picked
> automatically.</cell id="cell-11">
<cell id="cell-12"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 2. Build ONE program for every engine

`fast` runs an ELF on QEMU alone - a **transparent passthrough**: the program's
own input/output flows straight through and QEMU's exit code is propagated.

Historically you needed a different build per engine: QEMU wanted `-mvh`
(semihosting), which vsim cannot service. This repo now ships a portable
runtime - the **vplat runtime** (`runtime/vplat_syscalls.c`) -
that talks only to devices BOTH engines model at the same addresses:

| Channel | Device | QEMU ae350 | vsim |
|---------|--------|------------|------|
| stdio (fd 0-2)   | UART2 16550 @ `0xf0300000`  | yes | yes |
| exit code        | SimControl @ `0xe0080000`   | yes | yes |
| file io (fd > 2) | HTIF command @ `0xe0080010` | yes | yes |

No semihosting and no "which engine am I on" probe (a hybrid run migrates the
process between engines mid-run, so any boot-time detection would go stale) -
one binary therefore runs on `fast`, on `cycle`, and across a `hybrid`
handoff.

The runtime ships prebuilt as `build/runtime/libandesim_runtime.a`
(build it with `bash scripts/build_all.sh runtime`). The compile command
then needs just two extra flags: `-B build/runtime` and
`-specs=andesim.specs`, which together pull in the runtime's startup
code, linker script, and libraries so the binary runs on every engine.
The `say_hello` function and the `roi_end` label delimit the region
section 4d will measure.</cell id="cell-12">
<cell id="cell-13">%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null     # sets HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN (also done by `source ./setup.sh`)
GCC="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc"
[ -x "$GCC" ] || { echo "toolchain missing - run: source ./setup.sh"; exit 1; }

cat > hello.c <<'EOF'
#include <stdio.h>

__attribute__((noinline)) void say_hello(void)
{
  printf("hello\n");
}

int main(void)
{
  say_hello();
  /* ROI end marker for hybrid --pc-end: the return point after the call. */
  __asm__ __volatile__(".globl roi_end\nroi_end:" ::: "memory");
  return 0;
}
EOF

make -C runtime TOOLCHAIN="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN" >/dev/null   # build the runtime library (once)

# vplat runtime: UART stdio + SimControl exit + HTIF file io; no -mvh.
"$GCC" -march=rv64gc -mabi=lp64d -O1 \
  -B build/runtime -specs=andesim.specs hello.c -o hello.elf

echo "built hello.elf:"; file hello.elf</cell id="cell-13">

built hello.elf:


hello.elf: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, UCB RISC-V, RVC, double-float ABI, version 1 (SYSV), staticall

y linked, with debug_info, not stripped

<cell id="cell-21"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 4. Model `hybrid` - the headline

`hybrid` runs two legs in one command:

```
QEMU1  -- drained state + shared memory -->  vsim
(fast-forward to the ROI)                    (measure the ROI, then drain)
```

The result is **window_cycles**: the vsim cycle count for the region, measured
as `vsim mcycle - qemu mcycle`. The result lines go to **stdout** (an
`[hsim mmap]` line, the `[... window_cycles] N` line, and a `PASS:` line); the
`[andesim] model=... engine=... trigger=...` banner goes to **stderr**. With
`!` you see both in the cell.

The **trigger** decides where the measured region begins and ends:

| Trigger | Profiles          | How the region is delimited |
|---------|-------------------|------------------------------|
| `marker`   | a kernel you mark | two HINT-NOP markers (`slti x0,x0,0x5A0/1`) compiled into the source |
| `pc`    | a kernel          | two explicit PCs you pass (`--pc-start`, `--pc-end`); a symbol or `0x` address |

> The absolute `mcycle=...` numbers are a free-running counter and differ on
> every run. The bracketed `window_cycles` value is the figure you care about,
> and it is deterministic for a given ELF + engine + trigger.</cell id="cell-21">

<cell id="cell-29"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>### 4e. Cross-check the run against a QEMU oracle (`--verify`)

There is no handback leg, so nothing after your ROI ever runs - what proves
the RTL executed the ROI *correctly*? `--verify` (default OFF) answers it
with a differential check: the same ELF re-runs on pure QEMU (the oracle),
the plugin drains the full architectural state at the ROI exit - sampled at
the exact pc where vsim halted - and the driver diffs the two drains field
by field:

- **compared**: pc, all 32 GPRs, the FPRs, the V CSRs and full vector
  registers;
- **excluded**: `mcycle`/`minstret` (the engines count differently by
  design) and the passthrough M-CSRs/PMP (vsim copies those from the entry
  snapshot, so there is nothing fresh to compare).

Any divergence prints a `[state-diff] field: ref=... got=...` line per
mismatching field and the run exits non-zero. A clean run costs one extra
MHz-class QEMU pass - cheap next to the vsim leg. **Trigger constraint**: `--verify` needs `--mode hybrid` with `--trigger marker|pc`.</cell id="cell-29">

lines:
`[state-diff] PASS: 109 fields match` is the field-by-field compare,
`[verify] PASS` the verdict. The oracle's stderr banner shows the sample

For regression testing, pass `--verify` on a hybrid run; the hybrid e2e

Details (and the failure anatomy) in `docs/USER_GUIDE.md` section 4.7.</cell id="cell-31">
<cell id="cell-32"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>### 4f. Localize a divergence with checkpoint co-sim (`--cosim`)

`--verify` (4e) tells you THAT the vsim leg diverged; `--cosim` tells you
roughly WHERE. It is a developer tool (hidden from the release help; set
`ANDESIM_DEV=1` to see it in `run --help`):

```
hybrid run:  QEMU1 -> vsim: ..N insns..|..N insns..|.. exit
                              ckpt 1      ckpt 2      final drain
oracle run:  pure QEMU, drains at the SAME retire counts
diff ckpt k vs ckpt k -> first mismatch = the bad N-instruction window
```

Every N retired instructions (default 10000, `--cosim-interval` overrides)
the vsim leg halts the hart over DMI, drains a full architectural
checkpoint, and resumes. The driver reads each checkpoint's
`minstret - entry.minstret` (the exact post-entry retire count), re-runs
the ELF on pure QEMU with the plugin draining at those same counts, and
diffs checkpoint against checkpoint with the `state-diff` policy. The two
runs never share memory: the oracle replays the same deterministic program
from boot on its own RAM, so the shared mmap needs no change.</cell id="cell-32">
<cell id="cell-33">!andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium --cosim --cosim-interval 500 tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul.elf</cell id="cell-33">

<cell id="cell-34"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>The GEMM ROI retires 1692 instructions, so interval 500 gives three
checkpoints; `[cosim] PASS` means all three AND the final state match the
oracle. On a divergence you instead get the mismatching fields and the
window that contains the first bad instruction:

```
[state-diff] x12: ref=0x2a got=0x2b
[cosim] FAIL: divergence in window 2 (retires 500..1000 after entry)
```

Re-run with a smaller `--cosim-interval` to shrink the window.

**Limitations of this co-sim design**

- **Window granularity, not instruction granularity.** A divergence is
  bracketed to one N-instruction window; finding the exact instruction
  means re-running with a smaller N. Intervals near the DMI halt overshoot
  (tens of instructions) are not meaningful.
- **Registers only - memory is not compared.** Each checkpoint covers pc,
  GPRs, FPRs, V CSRs and vector registers. A wrong store is caught only
  later, when the bad value is loaded back into a register.
- **No cycle figure.** Every checkpoint adds a DMI halt + drain + resume
  on the vsim leg, which pollutes the vsim `mcycle` delta, so `--cosim`
  suppresses `window_cycles` entirely. Re-run without `--cosim` to
  measure.
- **`--trigger marker|pc` only, `--mode hybrid` only.** The oracle must
  arm on a code boundary; the icount trigger's window semantics differ
  between the legs. Exclusive with `--verify` (the final-state check is
  already included).
- **Single-shot, deterministic runs only.** The oracle replays the program
  from boot, so the pre-ROI path must be deterministic, and the ROI is
  assumed to be entered once (same assumptions as the hybrid run itself).
- **Counters are excluded from the compare** (`mcycle`/`minstret` differ
  between engines by design), as are the passthrough M-CSRs/PMP - same
  policy as `state-diff`.

Details in `docs/USER_GUIDE.md` section 4.8.</cell id="cell-34">
<cell id="cell-35"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 5. Picking an engine with `--engine`

`--engine <id>` selects which simulator to use. For `fast` it must be `qemu`
(the only functional engine). For `cycle` and `hybrid` it names one of the
`vsim:<cpu>` rows from `list engines`. Different CPU configs have different
microarchitectures and VLEN, so the same workload reports different cycles.

Try it yourself - rerun the marker example (section 4a) on a different core and
compare the number:

```sh
andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:ax45mpv_mp2 \
  tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul.elf
```

A heavier core simulates more slowly. If a leg exceeds the built-in 90 s per-leg
timeout, andesim stops it with `plan step 1: timed out after 90000 ms`; in that
case measure a smaller ROI or pick a lighter core.</cell id="cell-35">
<cell id="cell-36"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 6. Forwarding native engine flags with `--`

Everything after a lone `--` is passed to the engine **verbatim**; andesim does
not interpret it. For simple cases, use the dedicated `--gdb` flag instead:

```sh
# fast: QEMU gdbstub on port 1234 (default); pauses at startup for a debugger to attach.
andesim run --mode fast --gdb tests/fixtures/rt_c_hello.elf
# custom port:
andesim run --mode fast --gdb --gdb-port 2345 tests/fixtures/rt_c_hello.elf

# cycle: vsim JTAG on port 9104 (default) + ICEman in foreground (requires $ICEMAN).
andesim run --mode cycle --gdb --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium tests/fixtures/rt_c_hello.elf
```

`--gdb` is not supported with `--mode hybrid` (the two-leg pipeline cannot pause mid-handoff for a debugger).

For flags that have no dedicated wrapper — waveform capture, monitor console, or any engine-specific argument not exposed by andesim — use `--` passthrough:

```sh
andesim run --mode fast tests/fixtures/rt_c_hello.elf -- -gdb tcp::1234 -S
```

(Not run here — it blocks waiting for a debugger.)</cell id="cell-36">

## State coverage: what the wire format carries

Inventory view of the ROI rule above. Everything below is checked against
`include/hybrid/state_abi.h` (struct), the QEMU plugin drain
(`qemu_plugin/hybrid_handoff.c`), the vsim resume (`resume_driver.hpp`),
and the vsim drain (`state_drain.hpp`).

### Carried in `hybrid_state_v1`

- 32 GPRs, 32 FPRs
- `fcsr` (frm + sticky fflags; added 2026-06-12, closing L20)
- 13 M-mode CSRs: `mstatus, mepc, mtvec, mcause, mtval, mscratch,
  medeleg, mideleg, mip, mie, mcycle, minstret, satp`
- 2 Andes machine-setup CSRs: `mcache_ctl` (0x7CA), `mmisc_ctl` (0x7D0)
  -- the cache / misc enable crt0 writes at boot (added 2026-06-16,
  partially closing L21)
- PMP: 16 `pmpcfg` + 64 `pmpaddr`
- V extension: `vstart, vtype, vl, vlenb, vreg[32], vxsat, vxrm, vcsr`
- F13 warmup metadata: `mcycle_at_measure_start`, `minstret_at_measure_start`
- `reserved[192]` = room for ~24 more `uint64` (wire format is version 2
  since L11 widened `vreg[]` to 128 bytes per register)

### NOT in the wire format at all

- All S-mode CSRs: `stvec, sepc, scause, stval, sscratch, sie, sip,
  scounteren, senvcfg, stimecmp`
- HPM block: `mhpmcounter3..31`, `mhpmevent3..31`, `mcounteren,
  menvcfg, mcountinhibit, mconfigptr, misa, time`
- Every Andes-custom CSR EXCEPT the cache / misc pair above: `mmsc_cfg,
  micm_cfg, mdcm_cfg, mxstatus, mdcause, mnvec`, ... (`mcache_ctl` /
  `mmisc_ctl` are now carried). See L21.

### Carried but NOT restored into vsim

The QEMU1 plugin drains them into the struct, but `ResumeDriver`
writes none of them into the vsim hart. They are dead during the ROI:

- `satp` (L3) and `medeleg, mideleg` (L4) -- S-mode CSRs the M-only
  default engine does not implement. (`mscratch` left this set in L23;
  `mepc / mcause / mtval / mie / mip` left it in L24 -- all writable
  M-mode CSRs that round-trip now.) PMP is restored only for
  S/U-privilege handoffs (L6, 2026-06-13) -- without it an S/U ROI
  cannot fetch on a PMP-implementing core; M-mode handoffs keep PMP
  pass-through-only.

CSRs actually restored into vsim: `mstatus, mtvec, mscratch (L23),
mepc, mcause, mtval, mie, mip (L24), mcycle, minstret, fcsr,
mcache_ctl, mmisc_ctl (L21)`, plus
`dcsr.prv` (the privilege level, verified after write) and the PMP block
for S/U handoffs (`resume_driver.hpp`). The writable M-mode CSRs are
re-read at drain and compared by `--verify`, except `mip` (restored +
re-read but not compared -- its pending bits are hardware-driven and
diverge between the engines' clocks).

### Transport ceiling - why "all CSRs" is not free

Three surfaces, three ceilings:

| Surface         | Mechanism                                     | Ceiling |
|-----------------|-----------------------------------------------|---------|
| QEMU1 drain     | plugin reads by NAME from gdbstub XML         | only CSRs the QEMU fork advertises |
| vsim resume     | DMI Abstract Cmd + Program Buffer (by number) | RO / WARL / locked bits will not take arbitrary values |
| vsim drain      | DMI Abstract read (by number)                 | general for any readable CSR |

Two structural blockers to "all CSRs":

1. Wire format is a fixed C struct; `reserved[192]` fits about 24 more
   `uint64`. Reaching the full M + S + HPM + Andes set needs a v2 layout.
2. Semantics, not just bits. Restore order and side effects already bite
   (`mstatus.FS/VS` gating, `vsetvl` atomicity for `vtype/vl`). Writing
   `satp` flushes the TLB; Andes `mcache_ctl / mmisc_ctl` toggle caches,
   prefetchers and branch prediction -- exactly the CSRs that shape the
   cycle figure, which is why the cache pair is now transported (L21):
   restoring `mcache_ctl` at resume re-enables the L1 caches crt0 turned
   on, and it takes the write fine via the debug module
   (`write_csr_tolerant`). Other vendor CSRs may still be RO / locked and
   await the same recipe.

Verdict: extending the wire format to a bounded set in this way is
feasible - the L20 fix is the worked example (one `uint64` carved from
`reserved[]`, drained by name, restored via the existing
abstract-or-PB write, read back at drain). S-mode trap CSRs and a
chosen Andes microarch subset can follow the same recipe.
"All RISC-V CSRs including Andes-specific" is not feasible without
redesigning the wire format and lifting the entire ROI envelope (L2-L6).

## Tier 1 - Will break on the next real workload

### L1. No semihosting inside the ROI; vplat is the supported I/O path  (F-T1.1)

- When it bites: any C code calling `printf`, `malloc`, `_exit`, `fopen`, or
  anything that ends up in `libgloss` between `enter_vsim()` and
  `exit_vsim()`, when linked against a semihosting runtime (`-lgloss_vh`)
  instead of the shipped vplat runtime.
- What happens: libgloss emits the semihosting magic triple

### L25. ROI code that reads or writes time-variant CSRs produces engine-dependent results  (new 2026-06-15)

- **The rule**: code inside the ROI must treat `mcycle` (0xB00), `minstret`
  (0xB02), `mip` (0x344), and `time` (0xC01) as opaque.  No branches,
  arithmetic, or writes on these CSRs inside the ROI.
- **Why**: QEMU approximates both cycle and instruction counts with a CPI≈1
  model; vsim counts actual RTL pipeline cycles and retires.  `mip` pending
  bits (MTIP, MEIP, MSIP) reflect live timer/platform state that differs
  between QEMU's functional clock and vsim's cycle clock.  These values
  diverge at every architectural moment inside the ROI -- by construction,
  not by bug.
- **What happens if the rule is broken**:
  - *Branch on `mcycle`/`minstret`*: the `--verify` oracle (pure QEMU)
    takes a different branch than the hybrid run (vsim); the diff reports a
    GPR or PC mismatch.  The plain run passes; only `--verify` exposes it.
  - *Write `mcycle`* (e.g. `csrw mcycle, zero` to reset a performance
    counter): `StateDrain` re-reads the reset value at the exit marker; the
    reported cycle delta is near-zero or underflows -- silently wrong.
- **Where**: any `csrr`/`csrw` on `mcycle`, `minstret`, `mip`, or `time`
  between the entry and exit markers.
- **Demonstrated by**: `tests/fixtures/break_mcycle_write.S` (write corrupts
  delta), `tests/fixtures/break_verify_diverge.S` (branch diverges under
  `--verify`).
- **Distinction from L22**: L22 is about async interrupts in the lock-step
  DV path; L25 is about the hybrid measurement path and any code that reads
  or modifies time-variant state inside the ROI.
- **Status**: by design.  A static linter on the ELF could warn on in-ROI
  reads/writes of these CSRs (not built).

## State coverage: what the wire format carries

Inventory view of the ROI rule above. Everything below is checked against
`include/hybrid/state_abi.h` (struct), the QEMU plugin drain
(`qemu_plugin/hybrid_handoff.c`), the vsim resume (`resume_driver.hpp`),
and the vsim drain (`state_drain.hpp`).

### Carried in `hybrid_state_v1`

- 32 GPRs, 32 FPRs
- `fcsr` (frm + sticky fflags; added 2026-06-12, closing L20)
- 13 M-mode CSRs: `mstatus, mepc, mtvec, mcause, mtval, mscratch,
  medeleg, mideleg, mip, mie, mcycle, minstret, satp`
- 2 Andes machine-setup CSRs: `mcache_ctl` (0x7CA), `mmisc_ctl` (0x7D0)
  -- the cache / misc enable crt0 writes at boot (added 2026-06-16,
  partially closing L21)
- PMP: 16 `pmpcfg` + 64 `pmpaddr`
- V extension: `vstart, vtype, vl, vlenb, vreg[32], vxsat, vxrm, vcsr`
- `reserved[192]` = room for ~24 more `uint64` (wire format is version 2
  since L11 widened `vreg[]` to 128 bytes per register)

### NOT in the wire format at all

- All S-mode CSRs: `stvec, sepc, scause, stval, sscratch, sie, sip,
  scounteren, senvcfg, stimecmp`
- HPM block: `mhpmcounter3..31`, `mhpmevent3..31`, `mcounteren,
  menvcfg, mcountinhibit, mconfigptr, misa, time`
- Every Andes-custom CSR EXCEPT the cache / misc pair above: `mmsc_cfg,
  micm_cfg, mdcm_cfg, mxstatus, mdcause, mnvec`, ... (`mcache_ctl` /
  `mmisc_ctl` are now carried). See L21.

### Carried but NOT restored into vsim

The QEMU1 plugin drains them into the struct, but `ResumeDriver`
writes none of them into the vsim hart. They are dead during the ROI:

- `satp` (L3) and `medeleg, mideleg` (L4) -- S-mode CSRs the M-only
  default engine does not implement. (`mscratch` left this set in L23;
  `mepc / mcause / mtval / mie / mip` left it in L24 -- all writable
  M-mode CSRs that round-trip now.) PMP is restored only for
  S/U-privilege handoffs (L6, 2026-06-13) -- without it an S/U ROI
  cannot fetch on a PMP-implementing core; M-mode handoffs keep PMP
  pass-through-only.

CSRs actually restored into vsim: `mstatus, mtvec, mscratch (L23),
mepc, mcause, mtval, mie, mip (L24), mcycle, minstret, fcsr,
mcache_ctl, mmisc_ctl (L21)`, plus
`dcsr.prv` (the privilege level, verified after write) and the PMP block
for S/U handoffs (`resume_driver.hpp`). The writable M-mode CSRs are
re-read at drain and compared by `--verify`, except `mip` (restored +
re-read but not compared -- its pending bits are hardware-driven and
diverge between the engines' clocks).

### Transport ceiling - why "all CSRs" is not free

Three surfaces, three ceilings:

| Surface         | Mechanism                                     | Ceiling |
|-----------------|-----------------------------------------------|---------|
| QEMU1 drain     | plugin reads by NAME from gdbstub XML         | only CSRs the QEMU fork advertises |
| vsim resume     | DMI Abstract Cmd + Program Buffer (by number) | RO / WARL / locked bits will not take arbitrary values |
| vsim drain      | DMI Abstract read (by number)                 | general for any readable CSR |

Two structural blockers to "all CSRs":

1. Wire format is a fixed C struct; `reserved[192]` fits about 24 more
   `uint64`. Reaching the full M + S + HPM + Andes set needs a v2 layout.
2. Semantics, not just bits. Restore order and side effects already bite
   (`mstatus.FS/VS` gating, `vsetvl` atomicity for `vtype/vl`). Writing
   `satp` flushes the TLB; Andes `mcache_ctl / mmisc_ctl` toggle caches,
   prefetchers and branch prediction -- exactly the CSRs that shape the
   cycle figure, which is why the cache pair is now transported (L21):
   restoring `mcache_ctl` at resume re-enables the L1 caches crt0 turned
   on, and it takes the write fine via the debug module
   (`write_csr_tolerant`). Other vendor CSRs may still be RO / locked and
   await the same recipe.

Verdict: extending the wire format to a bounded set in this way is
feasible - the L20 fix is the worked example (one `uint64` carved from
`reserved[]`, drained by name, restored via the existing
abstract-or-PB write, read back at drain). S-mode trap CSRs and a
chosen Andes microarch subset can follow the same recipe.
"All RISC-V CSRs including Andes-specific" is not feasible without
redesigning the wire format and lifting the entire ROI envelope (L2-L6).

# Competition Landscape: andesim vs Dromajo, ImperasDV, gem5

A side-by-side look at four tools that get lumped together as "RISC-V
simulators" but actually solve different problems. This page is for
deciding *which tool answers which question*, not for ranking them on a
single axis.

**The one idea to take away.** Sort the four tools on two questions:

1. *What does it model?* -- a functional / ISA view (correctness only, no
   cycles), a cycle-approximate microarchitecture model, or the real RTL
   cycle-for-cycle.
2. *What is it for?* -- being the golden reference in design verification
   (DV), or producing performance numbers.

Dromajo and ImperasDV are **functional golden models for DV** (they check
your RTL is correct; they emit no cycle counts). gem5 is a **performance
model** (cycle-approximate, used before RTL exists). **andesim** is the
only one that pairs a functional fast-forward engine (QEMU) with a
**cycle-accurate model built from the real Andes RTL** (Verilator) and adds
DV co-simulation on top -- trading generality (Andes cores only) for an
integrated fast + cycle-exact + co-sim flow.

================= cell 1 markdown =================
## One-line role of each tool

| Tool | One-line role | Camp |
|------|---------------|------|
| **andesim** | Hybrid functional + cycle-accurate (real RTL) simulator for Andes cores, with fast-forward and DV co-sim | Cycle-accurate + DV, integrated |
| **Dromajo** (Esperanto / UCSC-MASC) | Open-source functional RV64GC golden model for RTL co-simulation | Functional golden model |
| **ImperasDV** (Synopsys, ex-Imperas) | Commercial instruction-accurate golden reference + DV environment (RVVI step-compare) | Functional golden model |
| **gem5** | Open-source architectural (cycle-approximate) performance simulator | Performance model |

**Golden model vs cycle model vs hybrid -- the distinction that matters:**

- **Dromajo / ImperasDV are functional golden models.** They do *not*
  produce cycle counts. You run them lock-step beside *your own* RTL
  simulator and they check the RTL's architectural state every instruction.
  They answer *"is my RTL correct?"*, never *"how fast is it?"*
- **gem5 is a performance model.** It produces cycle estimates from a
  configurable microarchitecture, but it is *not* your RTL -- accuracy is
  model-vs-silicon, and it is typically used *before* RTL exists. It answers
  *"how fast would this design be?"*, approximately.
- **andesim's cycle figure comes from the actual RTL** via Verilator, so
  it is cycle-accurate to the specific Andes core, while QEMU fast-forwards
  the uninteresting code so you do not pay RTL speed for the whole program.
  It answers *both* *"is the RTL correct?"* (co-sim) *and* *"exactly how many
  cycles?"* (RTL `mcycle`).

================= cell 2 markdown =================
## At a glance

`Yes` = first-class capability; `Partial` = technically possible but not
what the tool is built for; `No` / `n/a` = absent or not applicable. Where
useful, a cell adds a short reason in parentheses.

| Capability | andesim | Dromajo | ImperasDV | gem5 |
|------------|:---------:|:-------:|:---------:|:----:|
| Cycle-accurate timing from **real RTL** | **Yes** | No (no cycles) | No (no cycles) | No (modeled) |
| Functional golden model | Yes (QEMU) | Yes | Yes | Partial (atomic CPU, not a DV reference) |
| RTL co-simulation / step-compare | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| Fast-forward past the boring code | Yes | Yes (checkpoint) | Partial (fast ISS, but DV is step-by-step) | Yes (KVM/atomic) |
| Async-interrupt co-sim | No | Yes | **Yes** | n/a |
| Synchronous exceptions (traps) | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Instruction-exact divergence pinpoint | Yes | Yes | Yes | n/a |
| Boots an OS / Linux | Partial (QEMU leg) | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Follows the RVVI standard | No | No | **Yes** | No |
| Whole-program performance estimate | Yes (SimPoint) | No | No | Yes |
| Open source / free | Built on OSS | **Yes** | No (commercial) | **Yes** |
| Multi-ISA (beyond RISC-V) | No | No | No | **Yes** |
| RISC-V core breadth | Andes only | Any RV64GC | Any custom | Any |

================= cell 3 markdown =================
## Detailed comparison

| Dimension | andesim | Dromajo | ImperasDV (Synopsys) | gem5 |
|-----------|-----------|---------|----------------------|------|
| **Primary role** | Hybrid functional + cycle-accurate sim **and** DV co-sim for Andes cores | Functional golden model for RTL co-sim | Commercial RISC-V processor DV environment (golden ref + verification IP) | Architectural performance simulator |
| **What it models** | QEMU functional **+ the real Andes RTL** via Verilator | ISA functional (RV64GC) | ISA functional (ImperasFPM Fast Processor Model) | Configurable microarchitecture (in-order `Minor`, OoO `O3`) |
| **Accuracy class** | **Cycle-accurate** (real RTL) + functional | Instruction-accurate (no timing) | Instruction-accurate (no timing) | **Cycle-approximate** (model, not RTL) |
| **Co-simulation** | Lock-step DV (`dcsr.step`, zero slack) **+** ROI checkpoint co-sim vs QEMU oracle | Lock-step vs *your* RTL sim, linked as `libdromajo_cosim` via DPI | Step-compare vs *your* RTL via RVVI-TRACE, async-event aware | None -- it *is* the model |
| **Fast-forward (fastword)** | QEMU (MHz) runs to the ROI, hands arch state to RTL; SimPoint for whole-program | Checkpoint/restore: boot fast in SW, resume the checkpoint in RTL co-sim | Limited -- fast ISS, but DV is step-by-step, not skip-to-ROI | KVM/atomic fast-forward + switch-to-detailed; SimPoint sampling |
| **Speed** | QEMU MHz for the skip; RTL window ~0.01-0.1 MIPS; hybrid avoids all-RTL | Fast software sim (functional, many MIPS) | Fast functional ISS | `O3` ~0.1 MIPS; atomic/KVM far faster |
| **Bug localization** | First-divergence attempt index + ROI refine down to the instruction | First architectural mismatch vs RTL | Continuous arch-state compare; pinpoints instruction **and** async events | n/a (no RTL to compare against) |
| **Async interrupts in co-sim** | **No** -- out of scope (QEMU vs RTL take them at different attempt indices, so alignment breaks) | Yes -- injects external interrupts / debug on the fly | **Core strength** -- pipeline-sync tech for random async events | n/a (no co-sim) |
| **Synchronous exceptions (traps)** | Yes -- `ecall` / illegal / `mret` compared per attempt (`mepc`, `mcause`) | Yes -- full priv-1.11 trap model | Yes -- full trap / CSR compare | Yes -- priv-spec fault handling |
| **Boots an OS / Linux** | QEMU leg boots Linux; the cycle-accurate RTL leg measures a post-boot ROI (a full boot on RTL is impractical at ~0.01-0.1 MIPS) | Yes -- boots Linux, then checkpoint + resume in co-sim | Yes -- full-system reference model | Yes -- full-system (FS) mode boots Linux |
| **Follows the RVVI standard** | No -- own `state_abi.h` wire format + DMI compare (does not expose RVVI-TRACE) | No -- own `libdromajo_cosim` DPI API (predates RVVI) | **Yes** -- Imperas authored RVVI; uses the RVVI-TRACE interface | No -- a performance sim, not a DV step-compare tool |
| **Timing / cycle output** | **Yes** -- vsim `mcycle` delta (the headline number) | No | No | Yes -- modeled cycles |
| **ISA / target scope** | Andes RISC-V cores (the shipped RTL) | Any RV64GC core you wire up | Any RISC-V custom core; broad extension coverage | RISC-V **+ ARM / x86 / ...** |
| **Cost / license** | Internal Andes tool; built on open QEMU + Verilator | Open source, free (chipsalliance / UCSC-MASC) | **Commercial** license (Synopsys) | Open source, free (BSD) |
| **Maturity / ecosystem** | Andes-internal, focused | Open; used by BOOM, CVA6, etc. | **Most mature** commercial RISC-V DV; ISO 26262; authored the RVVI standard | Very mature; large academic + industry base |
| **Best at** | Cycle-exact perf on real Andes RTL **+** skip-ahead **+** DV, in one tool | A free golden model to stand up RTL co-sim | Sign-off-grade processor DV with async events | Pre-RTL design-space exploration |

*Speed figures are order-of-magnitude (public benchmarks); RTL/Verilator
~0.01-0.1 MIPS, gem5 `O3` ~0.1 MIPS, functional ISS many MIPS.*

================= cell 5 markdown =================
## Dromajo (Esperanto Technologies / UCSC-MASC)

**What it is.** An open-source RV64GC *functional* emulator built for RTL
co-simulation. Its semantic core descends from Fabrice Bellard's RISCVEMU /
TinyEMU, extended and bug-fixed to ISA 2.3 / priv 1.11. Released by
Esperanto; maintained on GitHub under `chipsalliance` (and a UCSC-MASC fork).

**Co-sim.** Dromajo is linked into *your* RTL simulator as a library
(`libdromajo_cosim`) and driven through DPI calls: the RTL retires an
instruction, Dromajo executes the same one, and their architectural state is
compared. First mismatch flags the bug. It is the *golden half* of a DV
setup -- you supply the RTL sim.

**Fast-forward.** Checkpoints capture architectural state, memory, the
interrupt controllers (PLIC/CLINT) and performance counters, so you can boot
Linux quickly in software, snapshot, and *resume that checkpoint inside the
slow RTL co-sim* -- skipping the boot you do not care about.

**No timing.** Dromajo emits no cycle counts; timing comes from your RTL,
correctness from Dromajo.

**vs andesim.** Dromajo is the free golden-model *half*. andesim bundles
the golden model (QEMU), a *cycle-accurate RTL model* (Verilator), and the
handoff -- so you get cycles *and* correctness without wiring up your own RTL
simulator. Dromajo is core-agnostic; andesim targets the Andes RTL.

================= cell 6 markdown =================
## ImperasDV (Synopsys, formerly Imperas)

**What it is.** A commercial front-end DV solution for RISC-V processors:
reference models, verification components, functional coverage, test suites,
and a debugger. Its reference is the **ImperasFPM** (Fast Processor Model),
*instruction-accurate*. Imperas was acquired by **Synopsys in late 2023**;
it ships as ImperasDV and through Synopsys Virtualizer.

**Co-sim.** Built on **RVVI** (RISC-V Verification Interface, the open
standard Imperas drove). The `RVVI-TRACE` interface connects the DUT's
instruction trace to the reference for continuous lock-step / *step-compare*
of architectural state. Its standout strength is **asynchronous events** --
interrupts and debug taken at unpredictable points -- handled via a pipeline
-synchronization technology. Async tandem-sim is the genuinely hard part of
processor DV, and this is ImperasDV's core competency.

**No cycles.** It is a functional sign-off reference, not a timing model.

**Cost.** Commercial license (via Synopsys).

**vs andesim.** ImperasDV is the gold standard for *processor DV
correctness*: core-agnostic, async-aware, broad extension coverage, and
certified for safety (e.g. ISO 26262 / automotive). andesim's lock-step DV
is deliberately narrower -- synchronous traps only, Andes cores, ~tens of
steps/s -- but it *also* yields cycle-accurate numbers and fast-forward,
which ImperasDV does not. The two are complementary: ImperasDV for broad
functional sign-off, andesim for cycle-exact performance plus lightweight
divergence hunts on the actual Andes RTL.

================= cell 7 markdown =================
## gem5

**What it is.** An open-source (BSD) *architectural* simulator spanning many
ISAs (RISC-V, ARM, x86, ...). CPU models range from `AtomicSimple` (fast,
functional) and `TimingSimple` through `Minor` (in-order) to `O3`
(out-of-order, detailed).

**Accuracy.** *Cycle-approximate.* gem5 is a configurable microarchitecture
model, **not** your RTL -- excellent for design-space exploration *before*
RTL exists, but its cycles are estimates (model-vs-silicon), not RTL
sign-off numbers.

**Speed.** The detailed `O3` model runs ~0.1 MIPS; atomic/KVM modes are far
faster and are used to fast-forward, with `switch_cpu` + SimPoint sampling to
apply the detailed model only on representative phases.

**No RTL co-sim.** gem5 *is* the model; there is no real-RTL comparison and
no DV step-compare role.

**vs andesim.** gem5 explores *hypothetical* designs; andesim measures
the *actual* Andes RTL. gem5 is faster to model and far broader (multi-ISA,
any microarchitecture you configure), but its cycles are estimates;
andesim's cycles are the RTL's real `mcycle`. Both use SimPoint for
whole-program numbers -- gem5 samples its own model, andesim samples real
RTL windows.

================= cell 8 markdown =================
## andesim (this project)

**Architecture.** QEMU (functional, MHz-level) **+ vsim** = SystemC +
Verilator running the *real Andes RTL* (cycle-accurate). A two-phase handoff
over a magic-CSR boundary: QEMU drains architectural state, vsim resumes,
runs the region of interest (ROI), and drains. The headline number is the
vsim `mcycle` delta.

**Fast-forward.** QEMU skips the uninteresting prologue at MHz and hands off
at the ROI (a marker HINT, a PC, or an instruction count), so you pay RTL
speed *only* for the window you care about. SimPoint mode clusters phases and
weight-combines them into a whole-program cycle estimate.

**Co-simulation (two modes).**

1. **Lock-step DV** -- `run --mode cycle --cosim`. Boot the same testbench
   on QEMU (the oracle) and the RTL (the DUT); single-step the RTL one
   attempt at a time with `dcsr.step`; diff architectural + trap CSR state
   per attempt; the first mismatch is the *exact* instruction. Zero slack.
   Built for small constraint-generated testbenches -- no fast-forward
   needed. Synchronous traps (ecall, illegal, mret) are supported;
   asynchronous interrupts are out of scope.
2. **ROI co-sim + refine** -- `run --mode hybrid --cosim [--cosim-refine]`.
   Checkpoint the RTL every N retires against a QEMU oracle at the same
   `minstret` deltas; find the first bad window, then subdivide it ~16x per
   pass down to the halt-slack floor to narrow where the RTL and oracle
   diverge.

**One tool, both answers.** Cycle-accurate performance *and* correctness
co-sim, on the real Andes RTL, in a single flow.

**Honest limits.**
- Andes cores only -- not a general-purpose RISC-V DV tool.
- RTL window speed ~0.01-0.1 MIPS; lock-step throughput ~tens of steps/s,
  which caps practical testbench size (~10-50k instructions).
- Async-interrupt co-sim is out of scope (synchronous traps only).
- Not RVVI-compliant -- it uses its own `state_abi.h` wire format and a
  DMI-based compare, not the RVVI-TRACE interface, so it does not plug onto
  third-party RTL the way Dromajo/ImperasDV do.
- The cycle-accurate RTL leg does not boot an OS; QEMU does the boot and
  fast-forward, and the RTL only measures a post-boot ROI.
- Open components (QEMU + Verilator), but the Andes RTL itself is proprietary.

================= cell 9 markdown =================
## Which one should I use?

| Your situation | Reach for |
|----------------|-----------|
| A free golden model to stand up RTL co-sim on *any* RV64GC core | **Dromajo** |
| Sign-off-grade, async-aware, safety-certified commercial DV across many cores and extensions | **ImperasDV** (Synopsys) |
| Pre-RTL design-space exploration, "what-if" microarchitecture, or non-RISC-V ISAs | **gem5** |
| Real cycle counts on **Andes RTL**, fast-forward to the hot region, and lightweight instruction-exact DV -- in one tool | **andesim** |

**They are not mutually exclusive.** andesim does *not* replace
ImperasDV's broad functional sign-off; it complements it. A realistic flow:
ImperasDV (or Dromajo) for exhaustive functional DV across the ISA, gem5 for
early architecture exploration, and **andesim for cycle-exact performance
plus quick divergence hunts on the actual shipping Andes core**.

================= cell 10 markdown =================
## Sources and caveats

Compiled from public information as of June 2026. The "Best at" and
positioning cells are an interpretation, not a vendor claim; competitor
capabilities evolve and cycle figures are order-of-magnitude. andesim rows
reflect this repository (`cosim_redesign.md`, `docs/USER_GUIDE.md`).

- Dromajo -- [chipsalliance/dromajo](https://github.com/chipsalliance/dromajo),
  [masc-ucsc/dromajo](https://github.com/masc-ucsc/dromajo),
  [Esperanto DV methodology (PDF)](https://riscv.or.jp/wp-content/uploads/EsperantoDVMethodology-Final-1106_compressed.pdf)
- ImperasDV -- [Synopsys ImperasDV product page](https://www.synopsys.com/verification/imperasdv.html),
  [Imperas + Synopsys RISC-V verification collaboration](https://www.design-reuse.com/news/53545/imperas-synopsys-risc-v-verification-collaboration.html),
  [RVVI adoption (Embedded Computing Design)](https://embeddedcomputing.com/technology/open-source/risc-v-open-source-ip/imperas-announces-the-latest-updates-to-rvvi-its-adoption-by-leading-risc-v-processor-developers)
- gem5 -- [O3 CPU model docs](https://www.gem5.org/documentation/general_docs/cpu_models/O3CPU),
  [gem5 v20.0+ paper (PDF)](https://inria.hal.science/hal-03100818/document),
  [Towards Accurate Performance Modeling of RISC-V Designs (PDF)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.09991)
